After the screening

Friday, 16 November 2035, almost midnight. After the premiere of the documentary “Répondre” at the Institut Lumière, Inès and Sami are sitting in a café in the Monplaisir district with Isabelle. Each of them gives their opinion of the film.
So? I was overwhelmed. It’s the truest film I’ve seen this year.
Of course it’s moving. But I found the beginning a bit slow. For the first twenty minutes you’re waiting for something to happen.
Exactly! The longer you wait, the more you want to hear the waltz. It’s as if the director were making us wait on the landing.
And the scene during which the screen goes black? I had never seen anyone dare to do such a thing.
That’s brilliant. Not only is it daring, but on top of that the whole audience fell silent at the same time.
Except your little cousin, who whistled at the end of the black!
Henri-Ion isn’t his cousin. But he whistled at the right moment, which is already a lot.
On the other hand, the soundtrack disappointed me a bit. There’s too much added music, whereas the waltz was enough.
You’re exaggerating. The only flaw, in my view, is the ending, which I didn’t expect at all.
Don’t say anything about the ending! There are people around us who haven’t seen it yet.
All right, I won’t give anything away. But what mark would you give it, Isabelle?
None. You don’t give a mark to a film in which you see your mother smile for the last time.
(after a silence) Then let’s simply say it’s a film that is like us. Imperfect, and all the truer for it.

1. The vocabulary of reviews
A good B2 review uses precise terms, not just “bien” and “nul”:
le scénario, l’intrigue
Le scénario est simple mais efficace.
the direction
la mise en scène, la réalisation
La mise en scène est d’une grande sobriété.
the actors
le jeu des acteurs, l’interprétation
L’interprétation est remarquable.
the image
la photographie, les plans
Certains plans sont d’une beauté rare.
la bande-son, la musique originale
La bande-son est un peu envahissante.
le rythme, le montage
Le montage manque parfois de rythme.
Verbs for effect: émouvoir, bouleverser, toucher (positive); décevoir, ennuyer, agacer (negative). “Ce film m’a profondément touché(e).” / “La fin m’a déçu(e).”

Don’t tell the ending! In French you say “divulgâcher” (Quebec) or “spoiler” (informal). In the exam: “sans rien dévoiler de la fin”.
3. Nuanced opinion
At B2 you are expected to weigh arguments, not just praise or criticise:
Of course, the pace is slow, but every shot has a meaning. (concession + contrast)
Not only is it daring, but on top of that it’s beautiful.
On the other hand, the soundtrack disappointed me.
It’s a pity that the ending is so quick. (subjunctive)
Despite a few slow passages, the film remains magnificent.

The ending, which I didn’t expect. (à + laquelle)
A film in which you see your mother smile. (dans + lequel)
The festival in which the film took part. (à + lequel = auquel)
Every shot has a meaning. None is useless.
Some viewers were crying, others were laughing.
For people, after a preposition, you can also use “qui”: “la réalisatrice avec qui j’ai parlé”. For things, only “lequel”: “la caméra avec laquelle elle a filmé”.

Huit secondes de noir

The “Eight Bars” exhibition closed its doors on Sunday 7 October 2035, at six in the evening. That day there was a queue all the way round the museum. At 5:59 p.m., the guards asked for silence in the room. Rose-Hélène opened the display case with the key Mrs Lacroix had entrusted to her. She took back Henri’s harmonica, as the clause provided, and put it in her pocket.

Before leaving, she played the three notes one last time, in front of Odile’s armchair. The three guards, who had heard the waltz more than four thousand times in eight months, answered together, whistling. One of them was crying. He said later that he had worked in that museum for twenty-two years, and that no exhibition had ever left such a gap as that one, the next morning.

But the story of the waltz was not over, because another woman had followed all of it very closely, without almost anyone noticing her. Her name was Léonie Garnier. She was thirty-four, with short hair and a small black camera that never left her. For two and a half years she had been filming the waltz. Wherever someone whistled it, Léonie was there, somewhere, at the back of the room.

She came from Saint-Étienne. She had made a few short films that nobody had seen, and she earned her living filming weddings. One evening in March 2033 she had come across the video of the silence on the Place des Terreaux by chance. She had watched it eleven times. On the eleventh, she had understood that she had found the subject of her first feature film.

She had another reason, which she only told at the end of the shoot. Her father had worked for forty years in a bicycle factory in Saint-Étienne. He whistled all day long, on the assembly line, tunes he made up himself and that nobody had ever written down. When he died, Léonie had realised that nothing was left of those tunes. Not a recording, not a note. She had promised herself never again to let a whistled melody disappear.

Julien had refused at first. He didn’t want a camera in his life, nor in his children’s. He had seen too many reports that turned people into characters, and characters into products. Léonie hadn’t insisted. She had only asked whether she could come to the Thursday orchestra, without a camera, just to listen. Julien had said yes, since anyone could come and listen.

She had come every Thursday for six months. She sat in the back row, listened, and left without a word. After six months she had brought croissants. After seven, she had started playing the triangle, very badly. After eight, Amina had made a spreadsheet to find out whether she could be trusted. The result was ninety-four per cent positive.

It was Rose-Hélène who had finally persuaded her father. She had told him that Léonie listened better than all the adults she knew, and that someone who listened so well couldn’t make a bad film. Julien had agreed, on one condition: that Léonie film the waltz, and not them. People, yes, but only when they were playing, whistling or keeping silent.

Léonie had respected the condition, or almost. She had filmed the Thursday orchestra, the La Duchère lime tree, the tree market. She had followed Amina and Bertrand to Dakar, paying for her own ticket, and had filmed quay number four without anyone seeing her. She had gone to Corsica to film Antoine’s bench, to Brittany to film Yves Le Goff, and to Bucharest to film the piano rising towards the balcony.

In Dakar, Ibrahima had been the only one to notice the little camera. On the second day he had come up to Léonie, leaning on his cane, and offered her tea. Then he had given her some advice. He had told her not to film him, because an old docker looked like nothing at all. She should film the sea, he had said, because it was the sea that had brought the waltz, and it was older than everyone.

In all, she had shot four hundred and twelve hours of footage. Now she had to make a ninety-eight-minute film out of it. It was, she said later, the most painful part of the work. Every shot she cut made her feel she was betraying someone. The further she got with the editing, the harder she found it to sleep. For five months she hardly left her editing room.

Her editing room was in fact a twelve-square-metre maid’s room on the sixth floor with no lift, in the Guillotière district. There were two screens, an old sofa, a slowly dying plant and a whole wall covered with little yellow notes. On each note there was a name, a place, a scene. In the end, a hundred and forty notes were left on the wall. There had been a thousand.

The neighbour downstairs, a retired man called Mr Ferrand, had come up to complain after the second week. He heard the waltz three hundred times a day through the ceiling, and he couldn’t take it any more. Léonie had apologised and bought headphones. A month later, Mr Ferrand came up again. He wanted to know why he couldn’t hear the waltz any more. He had got into the habit of whistling it while doing the washing-up.

The hardest part was the silence. Léonie had dozens of filmed silences: the one on the Place des Terreaux, the one at the town hall on the wedding day, the one on the Dakar quay, the one in the Bucharest street. She didn’t know which to choose. Each was beautiful. None was enough. One night, at three in the morning, she had an idea that made her leap off her sofa.

She would use none of them. At the third verse, in the middle of the film, the screen would go completely black. No image, no sound, nothing. For exactly eight seconds, the length of eight bars of the waltz played at Odile’s speed. It would be up to the viewers themselves to make the silence. The film wouldn’t show them other people’s silence. It would ask them for theirs.

The producer, a man in a hurry who had financed half the film, nearly choked when he saw the first cut. He said that eight seconds of black in a cinema was longer than an eternity. That viewers would think it was a breakdown. That projectionists would stop the film. That streaming platforms would cut the passage, as if it were a mistake.

Léonie didn’t give in. She replied that if the film lost those eight seconds it lost its meaning, and that she would rather not release it at all. The producer threatened, then negotiated, then finally gave in, on condition that a title card be added at the start of the film to warn projectionists. Léonie accepted the card. She wrote it herself: “The black is not a breakdown. It is a question.”

To reassure the producer, Léonie organised a test screening in a small cinema in Villeurbanne, in front of eighty viewers who knew nothing about the waltz. When the black came, a man shouted: “It’s broken!” A dozen voices answered “Shh!” at the same time. Then the audience fell silent. On the way out, the producer said the black was madness. But he added that he had never heard an audience fall silent so well.

That left the title. The producer wanted “The Sailor’s Waltz”, which he thought would sell better. Léonie had no idea. She asked Rose-Hélène, since she was the one who had found the title of the exhibition. Rose-Hélène thought about it through a whole meal. Then she said that the most important thing in the waltz was neither the sailor nor the silence. It was what you did after the silence.

So the film was called “Répondre” (“To answer”). Before showing it to the public, Léonie wanted to show it to the people in it. The first screening took place on a Thursday evening in October, in the Salle Hélène Morel, on a white sheet stretched between two music stands. The whole orchestra was there, the families, Mrs Roux, and a smell of popcorn that the school caretaker had made in the kitchen.

The reactions were as varied as the viewers. Julien spent the whole film hiding his face in his hands every time he appeared on screen, repeating that he had a ridiculous voice. Bernard Delorme found himself much older than he had thought. Mrs Roux declared that her blue dress was the most elegant in the film. Rose-Hélène complained that you could see her missing tooth.

Isabelle said nothing during the whole screening. For at the start of the film, for forty seconds, you could see Odile. It was a little video Julien had filmed on his phone in 2029, without telling her, one evening when she was whistling on the landing while watering her plants. Odile turned towards the camera, surprised, and smiled. Nobody but Julien had ever seen those images.

When the film was over, Isabelle went to see Léonie. She asked her how she had got that video. Léonie replied that Julien had given it to her only the day before, after months of hesitation. Isabelle turned to Julien. He said he had kept it to himself for six years, the way Henri had kept a lock of hair in a logbook, and that it was time to give it back.

The official premiere was set for Friday 16 November 2035, at the Institut Lumière, in the Monplaisir district. It was no coincidence. It was there, in the rue du Premier-Film, that the Lumière brothers had shot one of the first films in history in 1895: workers leaving their factory. Léonie said there was no better place to show a film about ordinary people.

But Léonie had another idea, crazier still. She wanted the film to be shown on the same evening, at the same time, in every place where the waltz had been played. Amina made a spreadsheet. There were four possible places besides Lyon: the drawing room of the Maison Stan in Bucharest, the village wash-house in Corsica, La Criée hall in Brest and Lamine’s mango tree in Dakar.

The problem was the time. Bucharest was an hour ahead, and Dakar an hour behind. Amina worked out that if it started at eight thirty in Lyon, the film would start at nine thirty in Bucharest and at seven thirty in Dakar. The eight seconds of black would therefore fall at exactly the same moment, everywhere. That was all that mattered.

In Bucharest, Sorina set up a projector in the drawing room of the Maison Stan, facing the back wall, next to the piano. Viorica, who had turned ninety-five in August, insisted on sitting in the front row. In Corsica, Marie-Ange and Paul Santoni stretched a sheet over the wall of the wash-house, the one where Rose-Hélène’s drawings had dried. In Brest, Nathalie booked La Criée. In Dakar, Lamine hung a white sheet from the branches of the mango tree.

At the Institut Lumière, the projectionist was called Marcel. He was sixty-eight and had been showing films in that cinema for forty-one years. Léonie had gone to see him the day before to explain the black. Marcel had listened without a word, then smiled. He had told her he had spent his life watching over films that never let the audience breathe, and that he had always been waiting for a film that would give him eight seconds of rest.

In Lyon, the cinema at the Institut Lumière had four hundred seats. They were all booked in eleven minutes. Guests came from all over France and beyond. Mariama had come from Dakar with Lamine, who was seeing Europe for the first time and thought November in Lyon felt like a punishment. He was wearing three jumpers, two scarves and a hat lent by Bertrand.

But wait, wasn’t Lamine supposed to be in Dakar, under his mango tree? He had thought of that. Before leaving, he had entrusted the sheet, the projector and the thirty-one children to his elder brother, a fisherman who had never seen a whole film but who had promised to make everyone respect the silence, even the goat. Lamine had left precise instructions, three pages long, in a spreadsheet Amina had corrected.

Yves Le Goff had wanted to come too, despite his ninety-one years and his wheelchair. Nathalie had said no, since La Criée needed him in Brest to introduce the film to the sailors. He had agreed, but reluctantly. Gérard Thiébaut had come from Mirecourt with a new child’s violin, the hundred and fiftieth he had made for the network. He wanted to give it to someone that evening, without yet knowing whom.

Mrs Roux had arrived first, an hour before everyone else, in her blue dress. She was eighty-nine and wanted to be sure of getting a good seat. Inès had come with Sami and Yanis. She was eighteen, in her first year of law, and told anyone who would listen that she would become a lawyer to defend trees. Clémence had come from Paris with her violin, in case anyone needed it.

There were also strangers, lots of strangers. People who had whistled the waltz one day in a museum, on a train, in a school playground. A nurse from Lille. A bus driver from Marseille. Two Japanese students who had discovered the waltz on the internet and had flown in for the occasion. And, in the back row, a man in a dark suit, alone, taking notes in a small notebook.

It was Paul Delmas, film critic for a major Paris weekly. He had the reputation of being the harshest critic in France. It was said that he hadn’t liked a film since 2019, and that he had made more directors cry than any producer. Léonie had recognised him as she came in. She had gone quite pale. Amina, who didn’t know him, had offered him a chocolate.

At eight thirty sharp, the lights went out in Lyon, Bucharest, Corsica, Brest and Dakar. Léonie’s title card appeared on the screen: “The black is not a breakdown. It is a question.” A few people laughed, without understanding. Then the first shot appeared: the landing of a block of flats, empty, filmed at dawn, with two doors facing each other. All you could hear was the distant noise of a city waking up.

The shot went on for a long time. Longer than any producer would have wanted. In the audience, some people started shifting in their seats. Then, from behind one of the two doors, very faintly, someone whistled three notes. The other door opened. It was Rose-Hélène, at six, in her pyjamas, harmonica in hand. She played the next three notes. And the title appeared: “Répondre”.

The film had no commentary. There was no voice to explain, no expert to analyse, no music to tell the viewers when they should be moved. There were only people playing, whistling, keeping silent. An eighty-two-year-old docker laying his hand on a rusty bollard. An old lady playing three notes with one finger. A child beating a jerrycan.

The viewers recognised one another on the screen. Every time someone appeared, there was laughter, murmuring, applause in a corner of the room. When Amina was seen counting the lime tree’s litres of water in a spreadsheet, the whole audience laughed. When Bertrand was seen playing for the first time in thirty-six years, the whole audience fell silent. Amina took his hand in the dark.

Then came the scene nobody was expecting. The one with the 2029 video. Odile on her landing, her plants, her watering can, her off-key whistled waltz. She turned round, she smiled, and the shot froze on her smile. In the audience, someone gave a little cry. It was Mrs Roux. Isabelle, sitting between Julien and Rose-Hélène, closed her eyes. Rose-Hélène put the harmonica in her hand without a word.

The film carried on, faster and faster, as if the waltz itself were speeding up. It moved from Lyon to Corsica, from Corsica to Dakar, from Dakar to Bucharest, following the three notes, whistled by more and more voices. A girl in Corsica. A sailor in Brest. A child in Dakar. A tram in Bucharest. And suddenly, in the middle of a phrase of the waltz, everything stopped.

The screen went black. Completely black. No more image, no more sound. In the cinema at the Institut Lumière, four hundred people found themselves in total darkness. For a second, some thought it was a breakdown, despite the card at the start. A man coughed. A woman whispered something. Then, almost at once, they understood. And silence fell over the room, deeper than any filmed silence.

At the same moment, in Bucharest, in the drawing room of the Maison Stan, sixty people were silent in the dark, around a piano. In Corsica, in front of the wash-house, a whole village was silent under the stars. In Brest, in La Criée, two hundred sailors were silent, and Yves Le Goff had closed his eyes. In Dakar, under the mango tree, thirty-one children were silent. So was the goat, for once.

Eight seconds. Eight seconds is almost nothing. It’s the time it takes to tie a shoelace, to read a sentence, to cross a small street. But in the dark, among four hundred strangers, eight seconds is very long. It’s long enough to think of someone you have lost. It’s long enough to hear your own heart. Several viewers said later that they had heard theirs.

At the end of the eighth second, before the image came back, a small voice whistled in the dark. Three notes. A little off-key, a little shaky, but at exactly the right moment. It was Henri-Ion, who would turn five in January, sitting on his mother’s lap. Nobody had asked him to. He had simply understood, all by himself, that someone had to answer, and that the someone could be him.

The image came back on the next shot, as if the film had heard Henri-Ion. In the audience there was huge laughter, then applause, right in the middle of the film, which is never done. In Bucharest, Sorina said later that Viorica had answered too, with one finger, on the piano, in the dark. In Corsica it was Lucas. In Dakar, Lamine’s brother. Nobody had arranged it.

The second part of the film was calmer. It showed the Corsican lime tree, green on one side only, and Antoine’s bench in the rain. In the audience, a little group of Corsicans applauded when Paul Santoni appeared, and Paul hid his face in his scarf. It also showed Mariama at the end of quay number four, her hand on the bollard. Sitting in the fifth row, Mariama looked at that woman on the screen as if she were a stranger.

Léonie didn’t watch the rest of the film. She watched the audience. She watched the faces lit by the screen, the hands seeking each other, the shoulders shaking. Above all she watched the back row, where Paul Delmas was no longer taking notes. His little notebook lay closed on his knees. She couldn’t see his face. The further the film went, the more she wanted to know what he was thinking.

The last scene took place once again on the landing from the beginning. But this time both doors were open. On one side you could see Julien’s flat, and on the other Odile’s, where Isabelle lived. Rose-Hélène crossed the landing from one door to the other, whistling. Henri-Ion ran after her. The camera didn’t follow them. It stayed on the empty landing, between the two open doors, until the credits.

The credits were long. Léonie had put in every name, absolutely every one. The Thursday musicians, the children of Dakar, the Corsican singers, the Brest sailors, the crane workers, the museum guards, and even the goat, under the name “a goat, Medina, Dakar”. At the very end, on a black background, there was one last line: “For Odile, who whistled off-key, and who waited for someone to answer.”

The lights came back on. Nobody moved for a long moment. Then the whole audience stood up at once to applaud. The applause lasted eleven minutes. Amina timed it. Léonie went up onto the stage, trembling, with Julien, who didn’t want to go up, and Rose-Hélène, who absolutely wanted to. Léonie tried to say something. All she managed to say was thank you, four times.

Then came a discussion with the audience. The questions were kind, for the most part. Léonie was asked how long she had filmed, how many hours she had cut, whether she had been afraid of the eight seconds. Then Paul Delmas raised his hand in the back row. The room fell silent. Everyone knew who he was. Léonie gripped the microphone so hard her fingers turned white.

He said the film was beautiful, of course. But he asked whether it wasn’t a little too easy. Whether a film full of old ladies, children and silences wasn’t simply trying to make people cry. Whether emotion wasn’t replacing cinema. He spoke calmly, without malice, like a teacher. The question was fair. That was exactly what made it so terrible.

Léonie didn’t know what to answer. It was Julien who took the microphone, to everyone’s surprise, because he hated speaking in public. He said Mr Delmas might be right. That the film was no doubt imperfect, sentimental, too long at the beginning. But that the waltz was imperfect too. That nobody had ever played it in tune. And that this was exactly why thousands of people had dared to answer it.

He added that if the waltz had been perfect, nobody would have dared to whistle after it. People don’t answer perfection, he said. They admire it from a distance, in silence, and then they go home. But when someone whistles off-key on the other side of a landing, you want to answer. Léonie’s film, he concluded, whistled a little off-key. And that was why it made you want to answer.

Paul Delmas made no reply. He nodded once and left before the end of the discussion. Léonie was convinced he hated the film. During the party that followed, in the foyer of the Institut, she couldn’t eat a thing. Gérard Thiébaut, who was still wondering whom to give his hundred and fiftieth violin to, finally gave it to one of the two Japanese students, who burst into tears.

Around midnight, in the foyer, Lamine took his kora out of its case. Bertrand took out his violin. They played the waltz together, among the glasses and coats, and the guests formed a circle around them. At that very moment Julien’s phone rang. It was Viorica, from Bucharest, who absolutely wanted a copy of the film for the music school. She said pupils had to learn silence before learning notes.

The next morning, Inès read the reviews aloud over breakfast at Julien’s, the way you read exam results. The Lyon daily spoke of “eight seconds of silence worth a whole film”. A national radio station said it was the most daring documentary of the year. A Bucharest newspaper had put Viorica’s photo on the front page. Amina started a spreadsheet of the reviews.

Paul Delmas’s article came out the following Wednesday. Léonie didn’t want to read it. It was Rose-Hélène who read it to her over the phone, slowly, stumbling over the difficult words. The title was: “I was wrong, by half”. Delmas wrote that he had come to Lyon to hate a sentimental film, and that he had left whistling three notes in the street, which hadn’t happened to him since childhood.

He stood by his reservations: the beginning was too slow, the added music sometimes intrusive, and some scenes more moving than necessary. But he added that he had spent thirty years reproaching films for leaving no room for the viewer, and that this one left him eight whole seconds. Eight seconds during which, for the first time in a long while, he had felt that a film was listening to him.

Rose-Hélène finished reading, then asked Léonie whether “by half” was good or not. Léonie was laughing and crying at the same time at the other end of the line. She replied that, coming from Paul Delmas, “by half” was worth far more than any compliment. Rose-Hélène said that in that case she would write him a letter to thank him. And she did, with three notes drawn in pencil.

Three weeks later, on a Thursday evening, a man in a dark suit walked into the Salle Hélène Morel during rehearsal. He sat in the back row without a word. Nobody recognised him except Léonie, who still played the triangle as badly as ever. During the silence of the third verse, the man fell silent like the others. Then, at the end of the eight bars, he took Rose-Hélène’s letter out of his pocket.

He looked at the three notes drawn in pencil. And he whistled them, off-key, very off-key, even more off-key than Odile. The whole orchestra turned round. Théo lowered his baton. Rose-Hélène, sitting next to Bernard Delorme, recognised her own letter. She took the harmonica and played the next three notes. Paul Delmas smiled. Léonie said later it was the best review of her life.

That evening, after rehearsal, Amina asked everyone to stay for five minutes. She had a spreadsheet to present. Bertrand sighed, because Amina always had a spreadsheet to present. She switched on the hall’s old projector. On the white sheet appeared a file everyone knew by name but nobody had ever seen. It was called “Us”. It was no longer empty.

There was a single row. In the first column it said: “Due date”. In the second: “9 May 2036”. In the third, headed “First name”, there were just three question marks. It took the orchestra a few seconds to understand. Bertrand was the last to understand. He dropped his bow. It was the first time anyone had seen him lose his composure in public.

The hall exploded with joy. Bernard Delorme played a fanfare on the trumpet. The bus driver and the baker hugged without knowing why. Léonie was sorry she didn’t have her camera. Rose-Hélène asked whether she could teach the baby the harmonica. Amina replied that it was already planned, row fourteen. And Bertrand, who had picked up his bow, played the waltz, trembling, more off-key than ever.

In the weeks that followed, the baby’s name became the Thursday orchestra’s favourite topic. Everyone had an idea. Bernard suggested Monique, like his wife. The baker suggested Baptiste, like himself. Rose-Hélène suggested Odile if it was a girl and Henri if it was a boy, or both at once. Amina listened to everyone and wrote nothing down. She said the third column would stay empty until May, and that this was exactly what made it so beautiful.

“Répondre” came out in cinemas the following January. It was shown in seventeen countries, in big cinemas and village halls, on festival screens and on sheets stretched between two trees. Everywhere, during the eight seconds of black, the audience fell silent. And everywhere, or almost, someone ended up whistling three notes in the dark before the image came back.

One January evening, Julien came home late from work. The building in the rue d’Austerlitz was silent. On the landing, both doors were closed. He stood still for a moment, his keys in his hand, as in the film’s first shot. Then, from behind the door opposite, very faintly, someone whistled three notes. Perhaps it was Isabelle. Perhaps it was Rose-Hélène. Julien didn’t try to find out who. He answered.

The review of the documentary “Répondre”, published by a Lyon newspaper the day after the premiere. Notice the structure: hook, summary, analysis, reservations, verdict. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
« Répondre » : huit secondes de silence qui valent un film
There are films we watch, and others that watch us. “Répondre”, Léonie Garnier’s first documentary, undoubtedly belongs to the second category.

The film tells the story of a waltz composed by a sailor who couldn’t read music, and which thousands of people now whistle from Lyon to Dakar, by way of Corsica and Bucharest. Without giving away the ending, let’s say that you no longer look at your landing in the same way when you leave the cinema.

What strikes you first is the restraint of the direction. No commentary, no experts: only faces, hands, instruments. Not only does the director never judge her characters, she also gives them time to exist.

The scene everyone will talk about is the one during which the screen goes black, without any sound, for eight long seconds. The longer the black lasts, the more intense the silence in the cinema becomes. It is all the more daring because no distributor would have accepted such an idea ten years ago.
Admittedly, the film has a few flaws. The beginning lacks pace somewhat, and it is a pity that the added music is sometimes intrusive, whereas the waltz was enough on its own.

But these reservations weigh little against the emotion that grips the viewer. In short, “Répondre” is an imperfect film, like its characters, and all the more precious for it. A must-see — and a must-whistle on the way out.
